title: Manual Training High School and Mr. Collins's little band
summary: He finished high school at 16, read widely, and Mr. Collins formed a school band with him on piano, rehearsing at his house; they played Christmas dates for about 80 cents a day.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: So when did you first really be able to play some with all that opposition?
I'll tell you what happened. The --
Which school was this where you --
This was at Manual Training High School in Muskogee. So I'm getting around my senior year. I finished high school pretty young. I finished it at 16, and--

Well, they thought I was. But the only thing that really helped me -- they thought I was a good student because during that time I would read and I never did do any studying. I did very little studying, but I did a lot of reading and I was lucky, whatever I was reading about, went along with classes and whatever they came up with, I was up on it, and that's how I -- you know what I mean. They thought
I was smart, but I wasn't.

It's lucky I was reading the right things, you know, and so anyway, that was getting around my, you know, senior year, and so this fellow Mr. Collins -- you know, the one that had practically forced me to play there in school, he told me he was going to get a little group together and he says, "I want you to play the piano." And he got saxaphone, I think he had two trumpets and a couple of saxophones and a bass and a drum, you know, and he put me on the piano, you know, so I told him, I said, "I don't know nothing about this stuff." He says, "That's all right. Just come on."

So then he says, "The first thing I'm going to do, I'm going to have rehearsals out to your house." He knew who my people were, you know. So he had the rehearsal out to my house and so they thought, "Well, you know, maybe this ain't too bad. You know, Mr. Collins, he's teaching there and he teaches music." He brought these guys out here and he had a drummer, you know, but my folks enjoyed watching him drum and he'd be doing all this stuff and you know how --
Yes, they enjoyed the drummer, you know. So they enjoyed the drummer and they would just sit and so they figured, "Well, maybe it wasn't too bad," you know,

so he told them, he says, "Now, we're probably going to play some Christmas jobs and you know," so I told him he'd better talk to them because I knew they wouldn't let me do it. So they said, "Well, if it's with you, it's all right. But if it was anybody else, we wouldn't let him play."
So we did. We did, I think, about three or four Christmas dates, you know, and --
You could bring a little money --

Made a little change. I don't know what we made. We made about 80 cents each day, I think, 80 or 90 cents. But the funniest thing about it, he would tell me, they'd start playing and I would be sort of listening, some tune that I didn't know. So he'd turn around and say, "Compliment the blues!" I didn't know what he was talking about. "Compliment the blues!" "Compliment the blues?" I said, I didn't know what that was, so I'd just start hitting notes that I thought would sound all right with them. He said, "That's what I'm talking about."

And I -- you know how you can be so dumbfounded and then you're founded, you know. So I said -- that was it. I says, "He sure had a funny way of telling me what to do." I said, "I didn't realize it was that easy," you know? So I finished high school and after finishing high school, I decided
